name: Dana Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior marketer at a small skincare start-up, there are nine of us in a converted print shop. I do the social content, the product page copy, and I email skin-care creators to see if they'll try our serums. I use AI tools all day, every day, for first drafts, for sorting creator lists, for testing ten headlines before lunch. Then my boss Pia, she's one of the founders, tells me which of them sound like a robot, and she's usually right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the speed. I can try something in the morning and see by the afternoon if anyone clicked. What's hard is that I'm still not great at the actual judgement bit, knowing which idea is good, and the money. The founders say we have funding until next summer, and after that nobody really knows. I've got about two weeks of rent saved, and there aren't many beauty brands in this city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but over-sold, which I already say. I'd post a little thread about what AI is actually good for in marketing, like sorting lists and boring resizing. People like those posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the AI part barely matters in this one. The scary part is our funding ending next summer. A start-up that runs out of money doesn't care whether AI was hype or not, it just shuts the lights off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools to get more done and try to prove I'm worth keeping when the money gets tight. I'd start building a portfolio site with my best campaigns, just in case. And I'd go back to the tenants' group meetings, because rent is the thing that actually decides my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a knot about next summer. The AI bit feels like background noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if the funding doesn't come through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm job hunting in a city with maybe four beauty brands. I'd look at remote work for agencies, which pays badly. My girlfriend Noor teaches at a nursery, so we wouldn't starve, but it would be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent decides your life. What's the tenants' group doing about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pushing the council to cap rises in our block. Our landlord added twelve percent this year. That's more than AI has ever cost me.

say: I'd say AI tools are **useful but over-sold**.
I'd post a thread on what AI is **actually good for** in marketing.
think: I think the real threat is our **funding ending** next summer.
AI barely matters next to **rent** and a start-up that could shut.
do: Keep using AI tools to **prove my worth** to the founders.
Build a **portfolio site** of my best campaigns.
Go back to the **tenants' group** meetings.
feel: Uneasy, with a **knot** about next summer's funding.
S0.quote: A start-up that runs out of money doesn't care whether AI was hype or not, it just shuts the lights off.
fieldNote: Her worry comes from a **struggling start-up** and rent, not from AI.
She already uses AI daily, so even a **small change** doesn't scare her.
Her politics are local and practical: the **tenants' group** and rent caps.

steps.text: Use AI drafting tools to get more campaigns out each week
Build a portfolio site with her best campaigns
Rejoin the tenants' group pushing to cap rent rises

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when workers need a seat at the table, not after. I'd write about how the gains shouldn't just go to founders and shareholders. I'd still say I like the tools, because I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job as it exists now disappears, and the founders do it with tools and a freelancer. I'm good with the tools, but I'm not good at the judgement yet, and the tools are getting good at that too. I'm basically training the thing Pia will use instead of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead of it, quickly. I'd pitch Pia on making me the person who runs our AI setup end to end, content, creator lists, ads, and checks it all. On the side I'd sell that same setup to two or three small local shops for a monthly fee. And I'd ask Noor if we can move somewhere cheaper so we have room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weirdly excited and scared at once. Like being good at surfing right before a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you're good at the tools, why not feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because everyone will be good at the AI tools in two years, so being early is only worth something for a while. I want to cash that in before it runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge a local shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hundred and fifty a month to run their social posts and emails with AI and check it. The bakery near us posts once a month, badly. They'd probably say yes if it's cheap enough.

say: I'd say workers need a **seat at the table** before the change, not after.
I'd say the **gains** shouldn't only go to founders and shareholders.
think: I think my current **job disappears** into tools plus a freelancer.
I'm basically **training the replacement** the founders will use.
do: Pitch Pia to make me the **AI setup lead**.
Sell AI-run social posts to **local shops** for about 150 a month.
feel: **Excited and scared**, like surfing right before a storm.
S1.quote: Everyone will be good at the AI tools in two years, so being early is only worth something for a while.
fieldNote: She's the **early adopter** who knows her edge expires.
Her **side income** idea is concrete: the bakery near her flat.
She mixes **pro-worker views** with real enthusiasm for the tools.

steps.text: Pitch the founders to make her lead on the AI content setup
Sell AI-run social posts to local shops at 150 a month
Move with Noor to a cheaper flat
Write posts arguing founders should share AI gains with staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency income support and we need it this year. I'd be organising, not just posting, getting people from the tenants' group and other start-ups into one room. Public me would be very loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm out. If AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, then a junior marketer with two weeks' savings is the first line on the spreadsheet. The robots in 2031 don't help, because the only hands-on part of my job is packing the odd PR box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the two years building something people need face to face. I'd go part-time at the start-up if they'll let me, and train in something with hands and people, maybe as a tattoo artist's apprentice, because I draw and it's about trust. And Noor and I would probably move in with her sister to cut rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My body's already tense just picturing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tattooing would face robots too, around 2031. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but who wants a robot tattooing them? I'm guessing people pay extra for a human hand. It's a bet, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Noor's job at the nursery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nursery work is hands-on and about trust, so I think she's safer than me for a while. That flips us, she'd be the main earner. We'd need to talk about what that means for both of us.

say: I'd demand **emergency income support** this year.
I'd **organise** people from start-ups and the tenants' group, not just post.
think: I think I'm **out**: a junior with two weeks' savings is first on the spreadsheet.
The **2031 robots** don't help, since my job is screens, not boxes.
do: Go **part-time** at the start-up if the founders allow it.
Start a **tattoo apprenticeship**, drawing on my art skills.
Move in with **Noor's sister** to cut rent.
S2.quote: A junior marketer with two weeks' savings is the first line on the spreadsheet.
fieldNote: She acts fast: a **tattoo apprenticeship** is a bet on people wanting human hands.
She sees **Noor's nursery job** becoming the main household income.
Even under the worst picture she turns to **organising** others.

steps.text: Start a tattoo apprenticeship while working part-time
Move in with Noor's sister to cut rent
Organise start-up workers and tenants into one campaign group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's use it to change the law, maybe shorter working weeks or a share of AI profits. I'd be in every meeting about it. I'd still teach friends the tools, because hiding from them helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the same ending as the fast one, I just get to choose my exit. Like I said, the start-up probably goes anyway. Five years is long enough to learn a real trade and short enough that I'd have to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the tattoo apprenticeship in evenings within a year, and keep running AI setups for small shops to pay for it. I'd try to save one month, then two. And I'd push the tenants' group to start talking about income, not just rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy. Busy makes it easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep selling AI setups to shops while warning about AI. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. But the shops will use it anyway. I'd rather a local shop pays a local person for AI than a big platform. I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you give up on the tattoo plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm just bad at it after a year. I'm still not great at marketing judgement either, so I know what being slow at something feels like. I'd give it an honest year.

say: I'd say **five years** is a warning to change the law.
I'd keep **teaching friends** the tools, because hiding helps nobody.
think: I think it's the **same ending**, but I choose my exit.
Five years is long enough to learn a **trade** if I start now.
do: Start the **tattoo apprenticeship** in evenings within a year.
Keep selling **AI setups** to small shops to pay for it.
feel: Anxious but **busy**, which makes it easier.
S3.quote: I'd rather a local shop pays a local person for AI than a big platform.
fieldNote: She admits the **contradiction** of selling AI while warning about it.
Five years turns her **side business** into a bridge to a new trade.
She gives the tattoo plan **one honest year** before judging it.

steps.text: Start an evening tattoo apprenticeship within a year
Run AI social posts for small shops to fund training
Save one month of rent, then two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, so failure would be a choice. I'd be campaigning for retraining paid by AI companies, and for shorter weeks. I'd probably be loud about it at work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years is actually kind of good for me. I'd have time to get good at marketing, then use the tools to run my own little agency, then move on before it closes. I'd be 37, still young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the start-up or the next one for three or four years and get properly good. Then I'd turn the side business into a real one with Noor helping on the books. Tattooing becomes a slow hobby I'd keep up in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. Still a bit of worry about money, because there always is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hopeful, but you'd still be on thin savings for a few years. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't fully. Rent's still the thing. But ten years means a bad year isn't the end of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor does, I'm not sure. Ten years makes me think about it more seriously. With two years, I wouldn't.

say: I'd say with **ten years**, failure would be a choice.
I'd campaign for **retraining** paid by AI companies, and **shorter weeks**.
think: I think a decade is **kind of good** for me at 37.
I could build **my own agency** and move on before it closes.
do: Stay in marketing **three or four years** to get properly good.
Grow the side business into a **small agency** with Noor on the books.
S4.quote: Ten years means a bad year isn't the end of the plan.
fieldNote: She sees **opportunity** in a decade, but still lives on thin savings.
Time changes her **family plans**: children feel thinkable with ten years.
Her agency idea relies on **Noor** doing the books.

steps.text: Stay in marketing three or four more years
Grow the shop side business into a small agency
Talk with Noor about having children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no runway and no trade. What would help is a quick, decent income floor and paid apprenticeships, so a 27-year-old can learn a new skill without going into debt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about rent, and rent is the background to all of this. If housing were cheaper, I'd take every risk you described. Being good with AI doesn't pay the landlord when the job goes.

headlineQuote: Being good with AI doesn't pay the landlord when the job goes.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** junior marketer at a nine-person skincare start-up who uses AI tools all day.
She has **two weeks' rent** saved, lives with Noor, a nursery teacher, and fights rent rises.
She moves first: pitching an **AI setup role**, a side business and a tattoo apprenticeship.
She goes from anxious about funding to **alarmed** under fast AGI, and hopeful with ten years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with **no runway** and no trade to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A **quick income floor** and paid apprenticeships so she can retrain without debt.
